tweets.text:
You are half right, but the wrong half is the scary one. 

The notion that pricing kills the business has it backwards. Metered token billing is the profitable end of this thing, not the trap. Inference already clears roughly 70% gross margins, and the part that actually bleeds is the flat-rate consumer subscription, which every provider runs as a loss leader to buy scale. So the "charge enough and users run" fear is pointed at the wrong product. The unit economics on the token side are fine, and they improve as compute costs fall.

The financing worry is the more legitimate one. There is real leverage and real circularity in the plumbing. But "mountains of off-balance-sheet liabilities" is not the same thing as debt coming due next quarter.

These are long-dated lease and capex commitments, staggered over three to eight years, taken on by companies that remain profitable and are funding roughly two thirds of the build-out straight out of operating cash flow. The borrowing that does exist is investment-grade and still the minority of the spend. That is the shape of a capital cycle, the same one every railroad, telecom, and cloud buildout has worn before. 

It is worth watching. It is not a reason to panic.

Fear talks you into selling the whole complex at the bottom of a drawdown. Discipline has you trim the weakest, most levered names, keep the profitable compounders, and let the revenue prove or disprove itself on the tape. Such is the difference between managing risk and letting it manage you.
